title: Case #7: Double-Booked Opening Night
summary: Opening night, and two people hold tickets for the same seat. Find the duplicates, fix the data, fix the schema, and find who keeps selling seats that are gone.

steps.title: Case #7
body: Opening night of *The Lighthouse Keeper's Wife*. The house is full, the lights go down, and an usher finds **two people with tickets for seat A3**. Then B2. Then B4.

The old ticketing system has no constraint stopping a seat being sold twice. Before Harbor Lights moves to your new schema, Rosa wants the mess cleaned up, the schema fixed so it can't happen again, and the source found.
Each step starts from the data as the previous step left it. Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)`, `tickets(id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel, sold_at)`.

steps.title: Clue 1: the double bookings
prompt: Return every **show_id** and **seat** sold more than once, with the number of tickets (**sold**).
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)` and `tickets(id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel, sold_at)`.
solution: SELECT show_id, seat, COUNT(*) AS sold
setup: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE shows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, starts TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO shows VALUES (1,'The Lighthouse Keeper''s Wife','2026-12-04 19:30'),(2,'Gaslight Choir','2026-12-05 19:30');
CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, show_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id), seat TEXT NOT NULL, buyer TEXT NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, sold_at TEXT NOT NULL);
hints: GROUP BY both columns, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
steps.explain: Three seats on opening night, and one on the second night.

steps.title: Step 2: keep the evidence
prompt: For each double-booked seat, the **earliest** sale is valid and every later one must be voided. Before deleting anything, save the later tickets into a new table **`voided_tickets`** with all of the tickets columns.
`CREATE TABLE voided_tickets AS SELECT ...` makes a table from a query.
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)` and `tickets(id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel, sold_at)`.
solution: WHERE e.show_id = t.show_id AND e.seat = t.seat AND e.sold_at < t.sold_at
setup: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE shows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, starts TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO shows VALUES (1,'The Lighthouse Keeper''s Wife','2026-12-04 19:30'),(2,'Gaslight Choir','2026-12-05 19:30');
CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, show_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id), seat TEXT NOT NULL, buyer TEXT NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, sold_at TEXT NOT NULL);
steps.stateQuery: SELECT id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel FROM voided_tickets ORDER BY id
hints: A ticket is voided if another ticket for the same show and seat was sold **earlier**: a correlated EXISTS.
`CREATE TABLE voided_tickets AS SELECT t.* FROM tickets AS t WHERE EXISTS (...)`

steps.title: Step 3: fix the data and the schema
prompt: Delete the voided tickets from `tickets`, then create a **unique index** on `tickets (show_id, seat)` so a seat can never be sold twice again.
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)` and `tickets(id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel, sold_at)`. and your `voided_tickets`.
solution: DELETE FROM tickets WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM voided_tickets);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tickets_show_seat ON tickets (show_id, seat);
setup: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE shows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, starts TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO shows VALUES (1,'The Lighthouse Keeper''s Wife','2026-12-04 19:30'),(2,'Gaslight Choir','2026-12-05 19:30');
CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, show_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id), seat TEXT NOT NULL, buyer TEXT NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, sold_at TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE voided_tickets AS SELECT t.* FROM tickets AS t WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM tickets AS e WHERE e.show_id = t.show_id AND e.seat = t.seat AND e.sold_at < t.sold_at );
steps.stateQuery: SELECT 'ticket', id FROM tickets UNION ALL SELECT 'unique', (SELECT group_concat(ii.name) FROM pragma_index_info(il.name) AS ii) FROM pragma_index_list('tickets') AS il WHERE il."unique" = 1 ORDER BY 1, 2
hints: `DELETE FROM tickets WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM voided_tickets);`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tickets_show_seat ON tickets (show_id, seat);`. The data must be clean first, or the index can't be built.

steps.title: Name the culprit
prompt: Which sales **channel** sold the voided tickets? Return **channel** and the number of voided tickets (**voided**), most first.
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)` and `tickets(id, show_id, seat, buyer, channel, sold_at)`. and your `voided_tickets`.
setup: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE shows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, starts TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO shows VALUES (1,'The Lighthouse Keeper''s Wife','2026-12-04 19:30'),(2,'Gaslight Choir','2026-12-05 19:30');
CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, show_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id), seat TEXT NOT NULL, buyer TEXT NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, sold_at TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE voided_tickets AS SELECT t.* FROM tickets AS t WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM tickets AS e WHERE e.show_id = t.show_id AND e.seat = t.seat AND e.sold_at < t.sold_at );
DELETE FROM tickets WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM voided_tickets);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tickets_show_seat ON tickets (show_id, seat);
hints: A plain GROUP BY on the table you saved.
steps.explain: **SeatSwift**, a reseller, sold every single one, always a minute or two after the real sale. Its integration was reading a stale seat map and never checking. With the unique index in place, its next double sale will simply fail. Harbor Lights' contract with SeatSwift is under review.
